questions.prompt: What basic claim does Chapter 10 make about consumption?
choices: It is only about satisfying practical needs
It includes signaling beyond obvious luxury display
It is always a pure wealth contest

explanation.gentle: The chapter widens buying beyond simple need or luxury.
explanation.direct: Its main move is to treat consumption as a broader signaling system.
explanation.competitive: Buying is bigger than use and bigger than flashy wealth.

questions.prompt: Which familiar signaling pattern does the chapter keep but refuse to treat as the whole story?
choices: Conspicuous consumption
Academic research
Body language

explanation.gentle: The chapter keeps conspicuous consumption but places it inside a wider frame.
explanation.direct: Luxury display remains real without exhausting the theory.
explanation.competitive: Flashy spending stays in the model without owning it.

questions.prompt: Besides wealth, what can purchases signal in this chapter?
choices: Only hidden private feelings
Conscientiousness, adventurousness, and identity
Nothing if the product is useful

explanation.gentle: The chapter says buying choices can show traits and group fit as well as resources.
explanation.direct: Consumer signaling includes character and identity, not only money.
explanation.competitive: A purchase can advertise who you are, not just what you can afford.

questions.prompt: A team debates which client-facing purchase makes them look more careful and professional. Which chapter idea is most visible?
choices: Purchases can signal conscientiousness as well as serve a practical role
Only price matters in visible buying
Consumer signals disappear in work settings

explanation.gentle: The item is being read for trait signals as well as for use.
explanation.direct: Conscientiousness can ride on a purchase without replacing its practical function.
explanation.competitive: The object is doing the job and shaping the reputation.

questions.prompt: Why might students care which reusable bottle they carry if several options work equally well?
choices: Because the item can also signal values, identity, or group fit
Because hydration has stopped mattering
Because all school purchases are luxury goods

explanation.gentle: Visible objects can communicate more than their direct use.
explanation.direct: The bottle can function practically while still signaling conscientiousness or belonging.
explanation.competitive: The tool works and the tribe signal rides with it.

choices: Some purchases signal wealth
Buying can carry public meaning beyond utility
All consumption is only conspicuous luxury display

explanation.gentle: The chapter treats luxury display as only one piece of the larger pattern.
explanation.direct: It rejects the idea that all buying collapses into conspicuous wealth signaling.
explanation.competitive: The board is bigger than the flashy corner.

questions.prompt: How does Chapter 10 grow out of Chapter 9 on conversation?
choices: It moves display from speech into visible purchases and public taste
It abandons signaling and focuses only on utility
It argues consumer choices have no social meaning

explanation.gentle: After conversational display, the book turns to how buying can also display the person.
explanation.direct: Consumption continues the hidden-motive story by shifting public display from talk to goods.
explanation.competitive: The signal moves from speech to stuff.

questions.prompt: Why might someone choose an unusual item at a cafe or store even when a safer option would work?
choices: To signal adventurousness or identity as well as satisfy the practical need
Because usefulness no longer matters at all
Because every unusual choice is secretly more efficient

explanation.gentle: The chapter says consumer choices can project boldness alongside use.
explanation.direct: A purchase can meet a need while also signaling novelty-seeking or self-concept.
explanation.competitive: The buyer can get the thing and the image in one move.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter insist that utility and signaling can coexist in one purchase?
choices: Because one object can solve a problem while also carrying public meaning
Because social meaning appears only when products stop being useful
Because utility and display always cancel one another out

explanation.gentle: The chapter's main tension is overlap, not replacement.
explanation.direct: A visible item can be practical and socially expressive at the same time.
explanation.competitive: The tool can work while the signal rides.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest bridge from Chapter 10 into Chapter 11 on art?
choices: If ordinary purchases already carry signal on top of use, art may intensify signaling through cost and impractical display
Art matters only when consumer signaling disappears
Consumption and art belong to unrelated parts of the book

explanation.gentle: The next chapter asks what happens when display value becomes even more visible.
explanation.direct: Art becomes the next step because it can amplify signaling through costliness and impracticality.
explanation.competitive: After use-plus-signal comes signal pushed harder.
